extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science and philosophy of science (readers interested in scientific method and epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Canonical canons and epistemic standards for when belief and inference are legitimate in scientific practice, and a theory of science that limits knowledge to sense-impressions/phenomena. Focuses on the appropriate scope of belief, tradition, inference, and the meaning of scientific 'reality' and individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 1 — Avoid belief where reason cannot be applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is impossible to apply man's reason, that is to criticize and investigate at all, there it is not only unprofitable, but antisocial to believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief is an adjunct to knowledge: a guide to action where decision is needful but probability is not overwhelming enough to amount to knowledge. Belief in spheres where we cannot reason is antisocial because such belief prejudices action in spheres where we can reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 2 — Infer only from known to like unknown in similar surroundings
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer what we cannot verify by direct sense-impression only when the inference is from known things to unknown things of the like nature in similar surroundings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: one may not infer an 'infinite' consciousness outside physical surroundings of finite consciousness; one may not infer 'man in the moon' merely by likeness if the physical surroundings differ. Inferences must be analogical and depend on similarity of nature and surroundings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 3 — Accept tradition only when continuous with present experience and credibly sourced
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer the truth of tradition when its contents are of like character and continuous with men's present experience, and when there is reasonable ground for supposing its source to lie in persons knowing the facts and reporting what they knew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the tradition that Wellington and Blücher won Waterloo meets these conditions; miraculous or fabulist claims (e.g., a miracle of Charlemagne, the adder story) do not. Evaluate tradition by content continuity with experience and credibility of original reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 4 — Do not adopt beliefs based on inadequate testimony as permanent conduct standard
rubrics_metrics.description: While it is reasonable in minor actions of life, where rapidity of decision is important, to infer on slight evidence and believe on small balances of probability, it is opposed to the true interests of society to take as a permanent standard of conduct a belief based on inadequate testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor, rapid decisions may permissibly use slight evidence; but habitual guides to important conduct require adequate testimony. Accepting inadequate-evidence beliefs as routine conduct weakens individual responsibility for important decisions (example: assuming a cab will be on the stand when catching a vital train).

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief's proper role — adjunct to knowledge and guide for action
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief is to be looked upon as an adjunct to knowledge: as a guide to action where decision is needful, but the probability is not so overwhelming as to amount to knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use belief pragmatically where immediate decisions are required and probabilities (not knowledge) must guide action. Avoid treating belief as a substitute for investigation where criticism and inquiry are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science's legitimate field — conceptions drawn from sense-impressions (phenomena/constructs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science deals with conceptions drawn from sense-impressions, and its legitimate field is the whole content of the human mind. Science only appeals to the world of phenomena — to immediate sense-impressions — with the view of testing and verifying the accuracy of its conceptions and inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the 'real world' for science as constructs made from immediate and stored sense-impressions (phenomena). Scientific statements should be grounded in sense-impression-based constructs, not asserted about unknowable 'things-in-themselves.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit inferences about causes/effects to the sphere of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The methods of classification and inference, which hold for sense-impressions and for the conceptions based upon them, cannot be projected outside our minds, away from the sphere in which we know them to hold, into a sphere which we have recognized as unknown and unknowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserting cause and effect (laws of phenomena) in regions beyond our experience is unwarranted. Be careful not to extend empirical laws to metaphysical domains; restrict causal statements to the domain of observable sensations and their lawful associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain agnosticism about 'things-in-themselves' — use 'sensation' to mark ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot know what lies beyond sense-impressions; to talk of 'things-in-themselves' producing sense-impressions is an unwarranted inference. By 'sensation' we shall understand that of which the only knowable side is sense-impression, expressing absolute agnosticism about whether sense-impressions are produced by unknowable things-in-themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt methodological agnosticism: avoid postulating shadowy unknowables (Matter, God, Will, Mind-stuff) beyond the sphere of sense-impression because they do not assist scientific explanation. Use 'sensation' to emphasize the boundary of the knowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'reality' and 'external world' in terms of projected sense-impression constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any group of immediate sense-impressions we project outside ourselves and hold to be part of the external world. As such we call it a phenomenon, and in practical life term it real. The real world lies for us in such constructs and not in shadowy things-in-themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between immediate sense-impressions (inside) and the constructed external world (projected combination of immediate + stored impressions). Recognize 'outside' vs 'inside' as practical distinctions tied to presence of immediate impressions (illustrated by Mach's visual-field example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality/identity criterion — persistence of grouped sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The individuality of an object consists for us in the sameness of the great majority of our sense-impressions at two instants of time. The 'reality' of a friend or an object consists for us in the persistency of the majority of the group of sense-impressions by which we identify him or it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify objects/individuals by continued similarity in grouped sense-impressions (examples: the ash-tree viewed at different moments; blackboard transformed into table). Do not invoke a hidden 'thing-in-itself' to account for identity — it lies beyond scientific conception and is unnecessary for practical identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge must be limited to thinkable phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'knowledge' is meaningless if applied to unthinkable things. Our only experience of thought is associated with the brain of man; no inference can legitimately carry thought any further than nervous systems akin to his.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of knowledge must remain within the sphere of what can be thought/experienced. It is absurd to assert limits of scientific method until a definition of 'knowledge' that includes unthinkable things is demonstrated; thus avoid claiming knowledge of entities beyond possible thought or sense-impression.
